newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom tells MMBG it quitting.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom tells MMBG it quitting.

text.p: German telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom AG said on Thursday it had informed members of the Multimedia Betriebs GmbH that it would quit the group as the euphoria over digital television begins to fade.
Shareholders in the MMBG consortium met at Telekom's Bonn offices. They issued a brief statement after the meeting but gave no details about the group's future.
"Deutsche Telekom will give its partners a proposal for further proceedings in the next few days," the statement said.

Telekom is MMBG's largest shareholder. Other shareholders include Bertelsmann AG, the publishing group, French pay TV group Canal Plus, Cie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT), the RTL TV network, public broadcasters ARD and ZDF and Daimler-Benz Interservices AG.
Telekom's departure from the MMBG group also sparked speculation that other members would exit. Bertelsmann and Debis strongly indicated on Wednesday that they would do so.
But there is more at stake than just the future of MMBG.

Bertelsmann and its Luxembourg partner CLT said they would abandon plans to launch a digital pay-television system, bringing an instant chill to the once-promising German digital TV market, where CLT and Bertelsmann have been investing vast sums of money for a showdown against the rival Kirch group.
"The CLT management will propose to its responsible supervisory boards that it concentrate on free TV markets," CLT said in a statement released late on Wednesday evening.
"The CLT management will thus advise the boards to cancel plans to bring a digital pay-TV programme bouquet known as Club RTL onto the market," added CLT.
In its statement, CLT said its decision to abandon the digital TV market for at least the time being had the "full support" of Bertelsmann subsidiary UFA.
CLT and UFA are planning to merge later this year.

"The first experiences with digital TV in Germany show that free TV will remain the dominant form of TV for the medium term," CLT said. Club RTL was to be the Bertelsmann/CLT answer to Kirch's DF1 system.

The company said that based on the sluggish demand for digital TV recorded by its rival Kirch, whose DF1 system has gotten off to a slow start since its July launch, it sees no point in investing further in the system for the time being.

"Our analysis has found that the chances of a further pay-TV system are extremely limited and a launch for Club RTL would make little sense at the moment," CLT said, referring to pay-TV network Premiere, with 1.2 million subscribers in Germany.
Kirch's DF1 is believed to have no more than 3,000 subscribers and will fall well short of its goal to have 200,000 subscribers by the end of the year.
MMBG was to market a common digital decoder and avoid a battle over technology standards in the new industry like the war between VHS and Betamax video recorders.
